body.text:
I lost fifty one pounds last year and my neck stayed behind.

The dress was the first time I really saw it.

My niece got married in April and I went to the mall by myself on a Tuesday morning because I wanted to be alone when I tried things on.

I am 67.

I had not bought a dress in a size 10 since the Clinton administration and I was close to proud of myself walking into that fitting room.

The dress fit.

That is the strange part.

It fit in the waist and it fit in the hips and I stood there in the three way mirror looking at the side view, which I had not done on purpose in maybe fifteen years.

My jawline was gone.

Not blurred.

Gone.

There was skin hanging under my chin that moved when I turned my head, and two soft rings across my neck that I swear were not there when I was heavier.

I sat down on that little bench with my purse on my lap for a while.

A salesgirl knocked and asked how I was doing in there and I said fine, thank you.

Here is what I was wrong about.

I had spent two years thinking the weight was the whole problem.

My doctor put me on one of those weekly shots for my blood sugar in the fall of the year before.

My A1c came down.

My knees stopped aching on the stairs.

I could get up off the floor after playing with my grandson without doing the whole production of rolling onto my hands and knees first.

Every number on every chart in that office got better and she was thrilled with me.

Nobody mentioned the skin.

I do not blame her.

She is a good doctor and she was watching my heart, not my neck.

But losing that much at my age is a strange kind of grief that comes with a win attached, and you cannot complain about it out loud because what are you going to say.

I got healthy and now I hate my chest in a v neck.

Because that was the other thing.

My arms wobbled when I waved.

The skin above my elbow folded like tissue paper when I lifted my hand to my face.

My chest looked crinkled above the neckline of every blouse I owned.

I started buttoning up.

I bought three scarves in May, which anyone from Georgia will tell you is not a May item.

What I did next was not smart and I will tell it anyway.

Over about five weeks I bought a neck firming cream from a department store counter, a tightening lotion with caffeine in it, a collagen powder for my coffee that tasted like a vitamin, and one of those rollers with the little needles on it that I used twice and then put in a drawer because it frightened me.

I did not add it all up until later.

It was a little over two hundred dollars.

The neck cream was the worst of it, because it came from a brand I have trusted on my face since I was forty.

The word neck was printed right on the box.

I used it twice a day for six weeks and my neck was moisturized.

That is all.

Soft on top and loose underneath, same as before.

I was ready to decide this was simply what sixty seven looks like and I should buy nicer scarves.

In June I flew out to Los Angeles to stay with my son and his wife for ten days.

Ji won is Korean, born in Seoul, came here for graduate school, and she is the one who taught me to make a proper rice.

On the Saturday she drove us to Koreatown to pick up groceries and she pulled into a little pharmacy first.

It was not a department store.

It was a pharmacy, with a glass counter and a man behind it in a white coat and shelves of things I could not read.

I was standing there holding a jar and reading the English side of the box when she looked over and said, oh, you want that one for the neck.

I said how do you know it is for the neck.

She said because that is where you start.

She said her mother put cream on her neck and her chest before she put anything on her face, and that her mother would have said we Americans have it backwards.

We buy a sixty dollar face cream and stop at the chin, and then we are surprised when the chin is the place everything shows.

I laughed and said something about it being too late for me anyway, and she said no, it is not, and then she explained it standing right there between the shelves better than anybody at a beauty counter ever has.

She said the skin does not run out of collagen.

That is the part everyone gets wrong.

Underneath the skin there are cells called fibroblasts, and their whole job, the only job they have, is making collagen and elastin.

After sixty they do not die off.

The message that tells them to get to work simply stops arriving.

They go quiet.

And everything they were holding up slowly lets go.

She said that is the loose skin under the chin.

That is the rings on the neck.

That is the crepey part above the elbow.

And when you lose a lot of weight quickly, there is suddenly less underneath to fill all of it out, so the slack that was being hidden shows up all at once.

The weight left.

The quiet cells stayed quiet.

Then she said the part that made me put the jar in the basket.

A lotion sits on top.

Water in, water out, and by lunchtime you are putting on more.

It is working on the surface.

The slack is not on the surface.

What she handed me works on the layer underneath, with peptides.

I know how that sounds.

Peptides is a word I assumed they made up to sell things.

But she walked me through it in plain terms.

There are seven of them in that cream, working three different ways at once.

One group relaxes the tension that holds a crease in the same place year after year, which is the needle idea without the needle.

One group is the signal, the message that stopped arriving, telling those quiet cells to start making collagen and elastin again.

And the third repairs the barrier so the skin keeps what the other two rebuild.

No retinol in it, which mattered to me, because the skin on my neck and chest is thin now and retinol on my face in the winter makes me flake.

I started it the night I got home.

Once a day, a small amount, smoothed upward from the collarbone to the jaw.

Then the chest.

Then the upper arms, because at that point why not.

It sank in in about a minute.

It has no smell at all, which I did not expect to care about and now I do, because it does not fight with the perfume my husband buys me every Christmas.

Week one, nothing.

I will be honest, I expected nothing, and I got it.

Week three I was in the car at a stoplight and caught the mirror at that angle you never catch on purpose, and the line along my jaw was there.

Not sharp.

There.

Enough that I turned my head twice to check.

Week eight was the Fourth of July cookout at my sister's.

I wore a sleeveless blue dress.

I had not worn sleeveless since 2013 and I did not announce it and nobody made a thing of it, which is exactly how I wanted it.

My daughter in law took a picture of me holding the baby, from the side, from slightly below, which is the shot I have deleted off my phone a hundred times.

I kept it.

It is on my refrigerator.

So for anyone who skipped down here, plainly.

Loose skin under the chin, on the chest and on the arms is not a surface problem, and that is why a drawer full of firming lotions never held.

The cells underneath that make collagen go quiet after sixty.

They have to be woken up, not moisturized.

The cream Ji won put in my hand is Olavita Tri Lift Peptide Complex.

Seven peptides on three pathways, including Syn Ake, Argireline and Snap 8.

Fragrance free, no retinol, made for the neck, jawline, chest and arms, and for the loose skin left behind after weight loss.

It is a Korean pharmacy formula, not a face cream with the word neck printed on the box.

It has 1,677 verified reviews at 4.8 out of 5, most of them from women over sixty, and it was reviewed by Michelle Mason, MD.

If you want to understand the three pathways before you spend a dime, they explain the whole thing here, with before and after photographs across six areas of the body instead of just the face.

Read how it works, then decide.

body.text:
I lost fifty one pounds last year and my neck stayed behind.

The dress was the first time I really saw it.

My niece got married in April and I went to the mall by myself on a Tuesday morning because I wanted to be alone when I tried things on.

I am 67.

I had not bought a dress in a size 10 since the Clinton administration and I was close to proud of myself walking into that fitting room.

The dress fit.

That is the strange part.

It fit in the waist and it fit in the hips and I stood there in the three way mirror looking at the side view, which I had not done on purpose in maybe fifteen years.

My jawline was gone.

Not blurred.

Gone.

There was skin hanging under my chin that moved when I turned my head, and two soft rings across my neck that I swear were not there when I was heavier.

I sat down on that little bench with my purse on my lap for a while.

A salesgirl knocked and asked how I was doing in there and I said fine, thank you.

Here is what I was wrong about.

I had spent two years thinking the weight was the whole problem.

My doctor put me on one of those weekly shots for my blood sugar in the fall of the year before.

My A1c came down.

My knees stopped aching on the stairs.

I could get up off the floor after playing with my grandson without doing the whole production of rolling onto my hands and knees first.

Every number on every chart in that office got better and she was thrilled with me.

Nobody mentioned the skin.

I do not blame her.

She is a good doctor and she was watching my heart, not my neck.

But losing that much at my age is a strange kind of grief that comes with a win attached, and you cannot complain about it out loud because what are you going to say.

I got healthy and now I hate my chest in a v neck.

Because that was the other thing.

My arms wobbled when I waved.

The skin above my elbow folded like tissue paper when I lifted my hand to my face.

My chest looked crinkled above the neckline of every blouse I owned.

I started buttoning up.

I bought three scarves in May, which anyone from Georgia will tell you is not a May item.

What I did next was not smart and I will tell it anyway.

Over about five weeks I bought a neck firming cream from a department store counter, a tightening lotion with caffeine in it, a collagen powder for my coffee that tasted like a vitamin, and one of those rollers with the little needles on it that I used twice and then put in a drawer because it frightened me.

I did not add it all up until later.

It was a little over two hundred dollars.

The neck cream was the worst of it, because it came from a brand I have trusted on my face since I was forty.

The word neck was printed right on the box.

I used it twice a day for six weeks and my neck was moisturized.

That is all.

Soft on top and loose underneath, same as before.

I was ready to decide this was simply what sixty seven looks like and I should buy nicer scarves.

In June I flew out to Los Angeles to stay with my son and his wife for ten days.

Ji won is Korean, born in Seoul, came here for graduate school, and she is the one who taught me to make a proper rice.

On the Saturday she drove us to Koreatown to pick up groceries and she pulled into a little pharmacy first.

It was not a department store.

It was a pharmacy, with a glass counter and a man behind it in a white coat and shelves of things I could not read.

I was standing there holding a jar and reading the English side of the box when she looked over and said, oh, you want that one for the neck.

I said how do you know it is for the neck.

She said because that is where you start.

She said her mother put cream on her neck and her chest before she put anything on her face, and that her mother would have said we Americans have it backwards.

We buy a sixty dollar face cream and stop at the chin, and then we are surprised when the chin is the place everything shows.

I laughed and said something about it being too late for me anyway, and she said no, it is not, and then she explained it standing right there between the shelves better than anybody at a beauty counter ever has.

She said the skin does not run out of collagen.

That is the part everyone gets wrong.

Underneath the skin there are cells called fibroblasts, and their whole job, the only job they have, is making collagen and elastin.

After sixty they do not die off.

The message that tells them to get to work simply stops arriving.

They go quiet.

And everything they were holding up slowly lets go.

She said that is the loose skin under the chin.

That is the rings on the neck.

That is the crepey part above the elbow.

And when you lose a lot of weight quickly, there is suddenly less underneath to fill all of it out, so the slack that was being hidden shows up all at once.

The weight left.

The quiet cells stayed quiet.

Then she said the part that made me put the jar in the basket.

A lotion sits on top.

Water in, water out, and by lunchtime you are putting on more.

It is working on the surface.

The slack is not on the surface.

What she handed me works on the layer underneath, with peptides.

I know how that sounds.

Peptides is a word I assumed they made up to sell things.

But she walked me through it in plain terms.

There are seven of them in that cream, working three different ways at once.

One group relaxes the tension that holds a crease in the same place year after year, which is the needle idea without the needle.

One group is the signal, the message that stopped arriving, telling those quiet cells to start making collagen and elastin again.

And the third repairs the barrier so the skin keeps what the other two rebuild.

No retinol in it, which mattered to me, because the skin on my neck and chest is thin now and retinol on my face in the winter makes me flake.

I started it the night I got home.

Once a day, a small amount, smoothed upward from the collarbone to the jaw.

Then the chest.

Then the upper arms, because at that point why not.

It sank in in about a minute.

It has no smell at all, which I did not expect to care about and now I do, because it does not fight with the perfume my husband buys me every Christmas.

Week one, nothing.

I will be honest, I expected nothing, and I got it.

Week three I was in the car at a stoplight and caught the mirror at that angle you never catch on purpose, and the line along my jaw was there.

Not sharp.

There.

Enough that I turned my head twice to check.

Week six my chest in a v neck looked smooth instead of crinkled, and I left the top button alone.

Week eight was the Fourth of July cookout at my sister's.

I wore a sleeveless blue dress.

I had not worn sleeveless since 2013 and I did not announce it and nobody made a thing of it, which is exactly how I wanted it.

My daughter in law took a picture of me holding the baby, from the side, from slightly below, which is the shot I have deleted off my phone a hundred times.

I kept it.

It is on my refrigerator.

So for anyone who skipped down here, plainly.

Loose skin under the chin, on the chest and on the arms is not a surface problem, and that is why a drawer full of firming lotions never held.

The cells underneath that make collagen go quiet after sixty.

They have to be woken up, not moisturized.

The cream Ji won put in my hand is Olavita Tri Lift Peptide Complex.

Seven peptides on three pathways, including Syn Ake, Argireline and Snap 8.

Fragrance free, no retinol, made for the neck, jawline, chest and arms, and for the loose skin left behind after weight loss.

It is a Korean pharmacy formula, not a face cream with the word neck printed on the box.

It has 1,677 verified reviews at 4.8 out of 5, most of them from women over sixty, and it was reviewed by Michelle Mason, MD.

If you want to understand the three pathways before you spend a dime, they explain the whole thing here, with before and after photographs across six areas of the body instead of just the face.

Read how it works, then decide.

My Korean daughter-in-law stood in my bathroom doorway and watched me do my entire face routine.

Cleanser.

Toner.

Vitamin C serum.

Eye cream.

Night cream.

Sunscreen.

Six steps.

About $340 worth of bottles.

When I finished, she pointed at my neck.

Then my chest.

Then my arms.

"In Korea," she said, "we never stop there."

I'd been stopping at my jawline for twenty years.

And everything below it looked twenty years older than my face.

Let me tell you what she taught me, because it's the one thing about skin that nobody in 
America ever told me.

I'm 52.

I live outside Charlotte, North Carolina.

I'm the office manager at a dental practice.

I've always taken care of my face.

My mother had beautiful skin, and she taught me young.

Wash it.

Moisturize it.

Never sleep in your makeup.

People guess my age wrong all the time.

Forty-four.

Forty-five.

They're guessing from my face.

My body is a different story.

Around 47, the skin on my chest went crinkly, like the top of a paper bag.

My neck got lines across it.

The backs of my arms went soft and papery.

There's a photo on our hallway wall from my 40th birthday.

I'm in a strapless black dress, and my husband Dale has his arm around me.

I look happy and smooth from my hairline to my hem.

I bought my first turtleneck the year I turned 48.

I now own eleven.

When Tyler and Ji-woo got married, it was June, outdoors, at a vineyard.

I found the perfect mother-of-the-groom dress.

Dusty blue, chiffon, sleeveless, a soft V at the neck.

I loved it on the hanger.

Then I tried it on at home under the closet light and saw my chest.

I took it to a seamstress and paid her $120 to add sleeves and raise the neckline.

She held the fabric against me and said, "Are you sure, honey? It's such a pretty dress the way 
it is."

"I'm sure."

At the reception, it was 91 degrees.

I spent the whole night dabbing sweat off my neck under that high collar, smiling for pictures.

I didn't ignore it.

I just treated it like a dry skin problem, because that's what I thought it was.

I bought the thickest body butter I could find.

Every night for a year.

My chest felt like a greased cake pan, and it looked exactly the same in the morning.

I bought a neck firming cream.

$78 for a tube the size of a lipstick.

I used it until it was flat.

Nothing.

I put my expensive face cream on my chest, thinking maybe the good stuff would work.

The jar ran out in two weeks, and I couldn't afford to keep that up.

I tried a body oil everybody on Facebook was talking about.

Eight different oils in one bottle.

It smelled like a candle store and left oil spots on my turtlenecks.

I even tried a retinol body lotion.

The skin on my chest went red and flaky for a week.

I couldn't wear a bra strap without it stinging.

Every one of them did the same thing.

Made my skin soft for a few hours.

Changed nothing.

My son Tyler married Ji-woo three years ago.

She's 31.

She's a pharmacist, and the most patient person I've ever met.

Last Thanksgiving, her mother flew in from Seoul for the first time.

Mrs. Park.

She's 63.

She walked into my house in a cream sleeveless blouse and a thin gold necklace that sat right 
on her collarbone.

Her neck was smooth.

Her chest was smooth.

Her arms were firm.

I was standing in my own kitchen in a black turtleneck.

Eleven years younger than her.

Before dinner, we did a family photo in front of the fireplace.

Ji-woo set the timer on her phone.

Afterward, everybody crowded around to look.

And Dale leaned over the screen and said, loud enough for the whole room to hear:

"Wait. You two are the same age?"

He meant it as a compliment to Mrs. Park.

Ji-woo said quietly, "No, Dad. My mom is eleven years older."

The room went silent.

Dale looked at me.

He realized what he'd just said.

His whole face went red.

"I'll go check on the pie," I said.

I went into the pantry, closed the door, and stood there with my forehead against the shelf of 
canned pumpkin.

I could hear everybody laughing about something else in the living room.

I could hear Dale say, "Where'd Janet go?"

I stayed in there long enough for the timer on the pie to go off.

Then I stayed a little longer.

Ji-woo found me.

She didn't say anything at first.

She just came in and closed the door behind her.

"Mom," she said.

She calls me Mom.

"Dale is an idiot. You know that."

I laughed and cried at the same time.

"I take care of myself, Ji-woo. I do everything right. I put six things on my face."

"I know," she said. "I've watched you."

Then she said, "Can I show you something tomorrow morning? Before my mother leaves?"

The next morning, she sat on the edge of my bathtub while I did all six steps.

When I finished, she pointed at my neck.

"In Korea, we never stop there."

She told me Korean girls are taught young that the face, the neck, the chest and the arms are 
all one skin.

You don't take care of half of it.

Then she explained the part I'd never heard.

"You think your chest is dry," she said. "It isn't dry. After 40, skin makes up to 70% less collagen. 
Collagen is the structure. It's like the wire frame inside a lampshade. Take the frame out, and 
the fabric wrinkles and droops, no matter how nice the fabric is."

She's a pharmacist.

She explains things to people all day.

body.text:
My Korean daughter-in-law stood in my bathroom doorway and watched me do my entire face routine.

Cleanser.

Toner.

Vitamin C serum.

Eye cream.

Night cream.

Sunscreen.

Six steps.

About $340 worth of bottles.

When I finished, she pointed at my neck.

Then my chest.

Then my arms.

"In Korea," she said, "we never stop there."

I'd been stopping at my jawline for twenty years.

And everything below it looked twenty years older than my face.

Let me tell you what she taught me, because it's the one thing about skin that nobody in 
America ever told me.

I'm 52.

I live outside Charlotte, North Carolina.

I'm the office manager at a dental practice.

I've always taken care of my face.

My mother had beautiful skin, and she taught me young.

Wash it.

Moisturize it.

Never sleep in your makeup.

People guess my age wrong all the time.

Forty-four.

Forty-five.

They're guessing from my face.

My body is a different story.

Around 47, the skin on my chest went crinkly, like the top of a paper bag.

My neck got lines across it.

The backs of my arms went soft and papery.

There's a photo on our hallway wall from my 40th birthday.

I'm in a strapless black dress, and my husband Dale has his arm around me.

I look happy and smooth from my hairline to my hem.

I bought my first turtleneck the year I turned 48.

I now own eleven.

When Tyler and Ji-woo got married, it was June, outdoors, at a vineyard.

I found the perfect mother-of-the-groom dress.

Dusty blue, chiffon, sleeveless, a soft V at the neck.

I loved it on the hanger.

Then I tried it on at home under the closet light and saw my chest.

I took it to a seamstress and paid her $120 to add sleeves and raise the neckline.

She held the fabric against me and said, "Are you sure, honey? It's such a pretty dress the way 
it is."

"I'm sure."

At the reception, it was 91 degrees.

I spent the whole night dabbing sweat off my neck under that high collar, smiling for pictures.

I didn't ignore it.

I just treated it like a dry skin problem, because that's what I thought it was.

I bought the thickest body butter I could find.

Every night for a year.

My chest felt like a greased cake pan, and it looked exactly the same in the morning.

I bought a neck firming cream.

$78 for a tube the size of a lipstick.

I used it until it was flat.

Nothing.

I put my expensive face cream on my chest, thinking maybe the good stuff would work.

The jar ran out in two weeks, and I couldn't afford to keep that up.

I tried a body oil everybody on Facebook was talking about.

Eight different oils in one bottle.

It smelled like a candle store and left oil spots on my turtlenecks.

I even tried a retinol body lotion.

The skin on my chest went red and flaky for a week.

I couldn't wear a bra strap without it stinging.

Every one of them did the same thing.

Made my skin soft for a few hours.

Changed nothing.

My son Tyler married Ji-woo three years ago.

She's 31.

She's a pharmacist, and the most patient person I've ever met.

Last Thanksgiving, her mother flew in from Seoul for the first time.

Mrs. Park.

She's 63.

She walked into my house in a cream sleeveless blouse and a thin gold necklace that sat right 
on her collarbone.

Her neck was smooth.

Her chest was smooth.

Her arms were firm.

I was standing in my own kitchen in a black turtleneck.

Eleven years younger than her.

Before dinner, we did a family photo in front of the fireplace.

Ji-woo set the timer on her phone.

Afterward, everybody crowded around to look.

And Dale leaned over the screen and said, loud enough for the whole room to hear:

"Wait. You two are the same age?"

He meant it as a compliment to Mrs. Park.

Ji-woo said quietly, "No, Dad. My mom is eleven years older."

The room went silent.

Dale looked at me.

He realized what he'd just said.

His whole face went red.

"I'll go check on the pie," I said.

I went into the pantry, closed the door, and stood there with my forehead against the shelf of 
canned pumpkin.

I could hear everybody laughing about something else in the living room.

I could hear Dale say, "Where'd Janet go?"

I stayed in there long enough for the timer on the pie to go off.

Then I stayed a little longer.

Ji-woo found me.

She didn't say anything at first.

She just came in and closed the door behind her.

"Mom," she said.

She calls me Mom.

"Dale is an idiot. You know that."

I laughed and cried at the same time.

"I take care of myself, Ji-woo. I do everything right. I put six things on my face."

"I know," she said. "I've watched you."

Then she said, "Can I show you something tomorrow morning? Before my mother leaves?"

The next morning, she sat on the edge of my bathtub while I did all six steps.

When I finished, she pointed at my neck.

"In Korea, we never stop there."

She told me Korean girls are taught young that the face, the neck, the chest and the arms are 
all one skin.

You don't take care of half of it.

Then she explained the part I'd never heard.

"You think your chest is dry," she said. "It isn't dry. After 40, skin makes up to 70% less collagen. 
Collagen is the structure. It's like the wire frame inside a lampshade. Take the frame out, and 
the fabric wrinkles and droops, no matter how nice the fabric is."

She's a pharmacist.

She explains things to people all day.

"Body butter is just more fabric softener," she said. "That's not you doing something wrong. You 
just never sent your skin the signal to rebuild the frame."

"I tried retinol," I said. "It burned."

"Retinol works on the frame," she said. "But body skin, especially the chest, is thinner than your 
face. Most women can't take it there every day."

"And the creams?"

"Mostly water. They sit on top. The water evaporates. Nothing gets down to where the collagen 
gets made."

"And the eight-oil one?"

She smiled.

"Eight kinds of fabric softener."

Then she went downstairs and came back with her mother's travel bag.

Mrs. Park pulled out a small glass bottle and handed it to me with both hands, the way you hand 
someone a gift.

CELMOR Silk Body Oil.

"Bakuchiol," Ji-woo said, tapping the label.

I'd seen that word on a face serum at Ulta.

I'd never once seen it on anything for the body.

Bakuchiol comes from a plant called Babchi.

Women in Japan and East Asia have used it on their skin for thousands of years.

"It tells the skin to start making collagen again," Ji-woo said. "And it stops the enzymes that are 
breaking down what you have left. Like retinol, without the burning. That's why my mother can 
put it on her chest every single day."

Mrs. Park nodded and said something in Korean.

"She says it's the first thing after the shower. Before anything else."

I read the label at the sink.

Jojoba, which is almost the same as your skin's own oil, so your skin soaks it right in instead of 
letting it sit there.

Macadamia, which brings back a fatty acid your skin stops making after 40.

Rosehip, which clears off the crinkly, dead top layer.

Evening primrose, argan and grape seed, for elasticity.

"Bakuchiol rebuilds the frame," Ji-woo said. "Everything else makes the fabric beautiful."

I'll be honest.

I didn't believe it was going to work.

I'd spent probably $1,500 on my chest and arms in five years.

I'd heard "this one's different" before.

But I'd also stood next to a 63-year-old woman in a sleeveless blouse the day before.

Mrs. Park left me that bottle.

I ordered more that night.

I put it on every morning, right out of the shower.

Neck, chest, arms.

In week one, it was the smell.

Warm and clean.

A patient at work asked what perfume I was wearing.

When I told her it was body oil, she didn't believe me.

It soaked in so fast I could pull my scrub top on right away.

At week three, I caught my chest in the bathroom light.

The crinkly paper-bag look was softer.

I leaned in close to make sure I wasn't imagining it.

At week five, the lines across my neck were faint enough that I bought a necklace.

At week six, Renee, one of our hygienists, stopped me in the break room.

She's 38.

She squinted at my neck like she was checking a patient's gums.

"Janet. Did you get something done?"

"No."

"Your neck looks different. Like, a lot."

"I started using a body oil."

"A body oil did that?"

She made me write the name down on a sticky note before she'd let me leave the break room.

At week eight, I wore a V-neck to Target and didn't think about it until I was back in the parking 
lot.

That weekend, I bagged up ten turtlenecks and drove them to Goodwill.

I kept one.

For skiing.

Dale noticed the empty hangers.

He stood in the closet doorway for a while.

Then he said, "I've been wanting to say I'm sorry about Thanksgiving for a long time."

"I know," I said.

"You look beautiful, Janet."

This time he said it to me.

This Thanksgiving, Mrs. Park flew in again.

I wore a sleeveless emerald green dress and a gold necklace.

Ji-woo set up the phone timer in front of the fireplace.

Same spot as last year.

Mrs. Park and I stood next to each other.

Both sleeveless.

When everyone crowded around the picture, Dale looked at it for a long time.

Then he said, "Janet. You look incredible."

Mrs. Park patted my arm and said something in Korean.

Ji-woo grinned and translated.

"She says now you know the secret. You can't give it back."

If you've been stopping at your jawline, I need you to hear me.

If you've got a closet full of turtlenecks, or you hold your hand over your chest in pictures.

You are not weak, and you didn't neglect yourself.

needed something different.

My Korean daughter-in-law stood in my bathroom doorway and watched me do my entire face routine.

Cleanser.

Toner.

Vitamin C serum.

Eye cream.

Night cream.

Sunscreen.

Six steps.

About $340 worth of bottles.

When I finished, she pointed at my neck.

Then my chest.

Then my arms.

"In Korea," she said, "we never stop there."

I'd been stopping at my jawline for twenty years.

And everything below it looked twenty years older than my face.

Let me tell you what she taught me, because it's the one thing about skin that nobody in 
America ever told me.

I'm 52.

I live outside Charlotte, North Carolina.

I'm the office manager at a dental practice.

I've always taken care of my face.

My mother had beautiful skin, and she taught me young.

Wash it.

Moisturize it.

Never sleep in your makeup.

People guess my age wrong all the time.

Forty-four.

Forty-five.

They're guessing from my face.

My body is a different story.

Around 47, the skin on my chest went crinkly, like the top of a paper bag.

My neck got lines across it.

The backs of my arms went soft and papery.

There's a photo on our hallway wall from my 40th birthday.

I'm in a strapless black dress, and my husband Dale has his arm around me.

I look happy and smooth from my hairline to my hem.

I bought my first turtleneck the year I turned 48.

I now own eleven.

When Tyler and Ji-woo got married, it was June, outdoors, at a vineyard.

I found the perfect mother-of-the-groom dress.

Dusty blue, chiffon, sleeveless, a soft V at the neck.

I loved it on the hanger.

Then I tried it on at home under the closet light and saw my chest.

I took it to a seamstress and paid her $120 to add sleeves and raise the neckline.

She held the fabric against me and said, "Are you sure, honey? It's such a pretty dress the way 
it is."

"I'm sure."

At the reception, it was 91 degrees.

I spent the whole night dabbing sweat off my neck under that high collar, smiling for pictures.

I didn't ignore it.

I just treated it like a dry skin problem, because that's what I thought it was.

I bought the thickest body butter I could find.

Every night for a year.

My chest felt like a greased cake pan, and it looked exactly the same in the morning.

I bought a neck firming cream.

$78 for a tube the size of a lipstick.

I used it until it was flat.

Nothing.

I put my expensive face cream on my chest, thinking maybe the good stuff would work.

The jar ran out in two weeks, and I couldn't afford to keep that up.

I tried a body oil everybody on Facebook was talking about.

Eight different oils in one bottle.

It smelled like a candle store and left oil spots on my turtlenecks.

I even tried a retinol body lotion.

The skin on my chest went red and flaky for a week.

I couldn't wear a bra strap without it stinging.

Every one of them did the same thing.

Made my skin soft for a few hours.

Changed nothing.

My son Tyler married Ji-woo three years ago.

She's 31.

She's a pharmacist, and the most patient person I've ever met.

Last Thanksgiving, her mother flew in from Seoul for the first time.

Mrs. Park.

She's 63.

She walked into my house in a cream sleeveless blouse and a thin gold necklace that sat right 
on her collarbone.

Her neck was smooth.

Her chest was smooth.

Her arms were firm.

I was standing in my own kitchen in a black turtleneck.

Eleven years younger than her.

Ji-woo set the timer on her phone.

Afterward, everybody crowded around to look.

And Dale leaned over the screen and said, loud enough for the whole room to hear:

"Wait. You two are the same age?"

He meant it as a compliment to Mrs. Park.

Ji-woo said quietly, "No, Dad. My mom is eleven years older."

The room went silent.

Dale looked at me.

He realized what he'd just said.

His whole face went red.

"I'll go check on the pie," I said.

I went into the pantry, closed the door, and stood there with my forehead against the shelf of 
canned pumpkin.

I could hear everybody laughing about something else in the living room.

I could hear Dale say, "Where'd Janet go?"

I stayed in there long enough for the timer on the pie to go off.

Then I stayed a little longer.

Ji-woo found me.

She didn't say anything at first.

She just came in and closed the door behind her.

"Mom," she said.

She calls me Mom.

"Dale is an idiot. You know that."

I laughed and cried at the same time.

"I take care of myself, Ji-woo. I do everything right. I put six things on my face."

"I know," she said. "I've watched you."

Then she said, "Can I show you something tomorrow morning? Before my mother leaves?"

When I finished, she pointed at my neck.

"In Korea, we never stop there."

all one skin.

the fabric wrinkles and droops, no matter how nice the fabric is."

She's a pharmacist.

She explains things to people all day.

"Body butter is just more fabric softener," she said. "That's not you doing something wrong. You 
just never sent your skin the signal to rebuild the frame."

"I tried retinol," I said. "It burned."

"Retinol works on the frame," she said. "But body skin, especially the chest, is thinner than your 
face. Most women can't take it there every day."

"And the creams?"

"Mostly water. They sit on top. The water evaporates. Nothing gets down to where the collagen 
gets made."

"And the eight-oil one?"

She smiled.

"Eight kinds of fabric softener."

Then she went downstairs and came back with her mother's travel bag.

Mrs. Park pulled out a small glass bottle and handed it to me with both hands, the way you hand 
someone a gift.

CELMOR Silk Body Oil.

"Bakuchiol," Ji-woo said, tapping the label.

I'd seen that word on a face serum at Ulta.

I'd never once seen it on anything for the body.

Bakuchiol comes from a plant called Babchi.

Women in Japan and East Asia have used it on their skin for thousands of years.

"It tells the skin to start making collagen again," Ji-woo said. "And it stops the enzymes that are 
breaking down what you have left. Like retinol, without the burning. That's why my mother can 
put it on her chest every single day."

Mrs. Park nodded and said something in Korean.

"She says it's the first thing after the shower. Before anything else."

I read the label at the sink.

Jojoba, which is almost the same as your skin's own oil, so your skin soaks it right in instead of 
letting it sit there.

Macadamia, which brings back a fatty acid your skin stops making after 40.

Rosehip, which clears off the crinkly, dead top layer.

Evening primrose, argan and grape seed, for elasticity.

"Bakuchiol rebuilds the frame," Ji-woo said. "Everything else makes the fabric beautiful."

I'll be honest.

I didn't believe it was going to work.

I'd spent probably $1,500 on my chest and arms in five years.

I'd heard "this one's different" before.

But I'd also stood next to a 63-year-old woman in a sleeveless blouse the day before.

Mrs. Park left me that bottle.

I ordered more that night.

I put it on every morning, right out of the shower.

Neck, chest, arms.

In week one, it was the smell.

Warm and clean.

A patient at work asked what perfume I was wearing.

When I told her it was body oil, she didn't believe me.

It soaked in so fast I could pull my scrub top on right away.

At week three, I caught my chest in the bathroom light.

The crinkly paper-bag look was softer.

I leaned in close to make sure I wasn't imagining it.

At week five, the lines across my neck were faint enough that I bought a necklace.

At week six, Renee, one of our hygienists, stopped me in the break room.

She's 38.

She squinted at my neck like she was checking a patient's gums.

"Janet. Did you get something done?"

"No."

"Your neck looks different. Like, a lot."

"I started using a body oil."

"A body oil did that?"

She made me write the name down on a sticky note before she'd let me leave the break room.

At week eight, I wore a V-neck to Target and didn't think about it until I was back in the parking 
lot.

That weekend, I bagged up ten turtlenecks and drove them to Goodwill.

I kept one.

For skiing.

Dale noticed the empty hangers.

He stood in the closet doorway for a while.

Then he said, "I've been wanting to say I'm sorry about Thanksgiving for a long time."

"I know," I said.

"You look beautiful, Janet."

This time he said it to me.

This Thanksgiving, Mrs. Park flew in again.

I wore a sleeveless emerald green dress and a gold necklace.

Ji-woo set up the phone timer in front of the fireplace.

Same spot as last year.

Mrs. Park and I stood next to each other.

Both sleeveless.

When everyone crowded around the picture, Dale looked at it for a long time.

Then he said, "Janet. You look incredible."

Mrs. Park patted my arm and said something in Korean.

Ji-woo grinned and translated.

"She says now you know the secret. You can't give it back."

If you've been stopping at your jawline, I need you to hear me.

If you've got a closet full of turtlenecks, or you hold your hand over your chest in pictures.

You are not weak, and you didn't neglect yourself.

You've been taking beautiful care of half your skin, and nobody ever told you the other half 
needed something different.

CELMOR Silk Body Oil uses Bakuchiol to tell your skin to start making collagen again, on your 
neck, chest and arms, in an oil that soaks in so fast you can get dressed right away.

Every morning, right out of the shower.

Right now, it's buy 2, get 2 free, plus free shipping.

And there's a 90-day money-back guarantee. If your skin doesn't look and feel firmer, you get 
every penny back.

And then go past your jawline.

P.S. Dale is banned from commenting on family photos until further notice. That was Ji-woo's 
idea. Mrs. Park seconded it.

P.P.S. The bottles are normally $40 each. With buy 2, get 2 free, that's $80 of oil you don't pay 
for, and the shipping is free too.
